claim: Anatomically plausible networks of functionally inter-connected regions have been reliably demonstrated at rest.
source: Anatomically plausible networks of functionally inter-connected regions have been reliably demonstrated at rest, although the neurochemical basis of these 'resting state networks' is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in the field of resting state networks.

claim: The neurochemical basis of resting state networks is not well understood.
source: Anatomically plausible networks of functionally inter-connected regions have been reliably demonstrated at rest, although the neurochemical basis of these 'resting state networks' is not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between levels of GABA within the primary motor cortex (M1) and the strength of functional connectivity across the resting motor network.
source: In this study, we combined magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and resting state fMRI and demonstrated an inverse relationship between levels of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA within the primary motor cortex (M1) and the strength of functional connectivity across the resting motor network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from combining MRS and resting state fMRI measurements.

claim: The relationship between GABA levels in M1 and resting motor network connectivity is neurochemically specific.
source: This relationship was both neurochemically and anatomically specific.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing specificity to GABA and not other neurochemicals.

claim: The relationship between GABA levels in M1 and resting motor network connectivity is anatomically specific.
source: This relationship was both neurochemically and anatomically specific.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing specificity to the motor network and not other networks.

claim: Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) decreases GABA levels within M1.
source: We then went on to show that anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), an intervention previously shown to decrease GABA levels within M1, increased resting motor network connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Stagg et al., 2009; 2011a).

claim: Anodal tDCS increased resting motor network connectivity.
source: We then went on to show that anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), an intervention previously shown to decrease GABA levels within M1, increased resting motor network connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: Network-level functional connectivity within the motor system is related to the degree of inhibition in M1.
source: We therefore suggest that network-level functional connectivity within the motor system is related to the degree of inhibition in M1, a major node within the motor network, a finding in line with converging evidence from both simulation and empirical studies.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in the study and is consistent with simulation and empirical studies.

claim: Resting state networks show correlated fluctuations in their resting signal.
source: These robust, distributed networks, most commonly detected using functional MRI, show correlated fluctuations in their resting signal and have revealed networks formed from spatially widespread but anatomically and functionally closely linked regions (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Snyder and Raichle, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox and Raichle, 2007 and Snyder and Raichle, 2012.

claim: Resting state networks are formed from spatially widespread but anatomically and functionally closely linked regions.
source: These robust, distributed networks, most commonly detected using functional MRI, show correlated fluctuations in their resting signal and have revealed networks formed from spatially widespread but anatomically and functionally closely linked regions (Fox and Raichle, 2007; Snyder and Raichle, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fox and Raichle, 2007 and Snyder and Raichle, 2012.

claim: Variation in the strength of functional coupling within resting state networks is highly sensitive to a wide variety of clinical, genetic, or cognitive states.
source: Understanding the basis of these resting state networks is of increasing interest, as variation in the strength of functional coupling within these networks has been shown to be highly sensitive to a wide variety of clinical, genetic, or cognitive states (Filippini et al., 2009; Pievani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filippini et al., 2009 and Pievani et al., 2011.

claim: Resting correlations have long been thought to be a functional marker of excitatory connections.
source: Resting correlations have long been thought to be a functional marker of excitatory connections (Vincent et al., 2007; Shmuel and Leopold, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vincent et al., 2007 and Shmuel and Leopold, 2008.

claim: Patterns of local oscillatory activity can emerge spontaneously in a coherent fashion across large networks with specific connectional architectures.
source: However, recent simulation studies have predicted that patterns of local oscillatory activity can emerge spontaneously in a coherent fashion across large networks with specific connectional architectures (Cabral et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cabral et al., 2011.

claim: Local neuronal dynamics depend on neurochemical inhibitory tone.
source: Such local neuronal dynamics depend on neurochemical inhibitory tone, as shown, for example, by changes in local activity within the primary motor cortices (M1s) caused by pharmacological manipulations (Hall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hall et al., 2011.

claim: If correlated activity spontaneously emerges through attractor dynamics in distant cortical regions, then extent of these functional correlations should be best predicted by local GABA concentrations.
source: If correlated activity spontaneously emerges through attractor dynamics in distant cortical regions, then extent of these functional correlations should be best predicted by local GABA concentrations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from previous findings about local neuronal dynamics and inhibitory tone.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant inverse correlation between functional connectivity within the motor RSN and GABA concentration within M1 in healthy young volunteers (r = −0.71, p=0.01).
source: Using ICA, we demonstrated a significant inverse correlation between functional connectivity within the motor RSN and GABA concentration within M1 (M1-GABA) in healthy young volunteers (r = −0.71, p=0.01; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was no significant correlation between M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN (r = 0.25, p=0.44).
source: There was no significant correlation between M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN (r = 0.25, p=0.44) (Figure 2D), and M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN was significantly less correlated than M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the motor RSN (Fisher's R-to-Z transformation, Z = −2.29, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In Experiment 1, M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN was significantly less correlated than M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the motor RSN (Fisher's R-to-Z transformation, Z = −2.29, p=0.02).
source: There was no significant correlation between M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN (r = 0.25, p=0.44) (Figure 2D), and M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the DMN was significantly less correlated than M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the motor RSN (Fisher's R-to-Z transformation, Z = −2.29, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was no significant correlation between motor RSN functional connectivity and M1-Glx (r = −0.35, p=0.36).
source: There was no significant correlation between motor RSN functional connectivity and M1-Glx (r = −0.35, p=0.36; Figure 2E), and the correlation between M1-GABA and motor RSN functional connectivity persisted when M1-Glx was co-varied out (r = −0.67, p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In Experiment 1, the correlation between M1-GABA and motor RSN functional connectivity persisted when M1-Glx was co-varied out (r = −0.67, p=0.03).
source: There was no significant correlation between motor RSN functional connectivity and M1-Glx (r = −0.35, p=0.36; Figure 2E), and the correlation between M1-GABA and motor RSN functional connectivity persisted when M1-Glx was co-varied out (r = −0.67, p=0.03).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, using seed-based correlation analysis, there was a significant inverse relationship between the degree of correlation between the two M1s and GABA concentration (r = −0.60, p=0.047).
source: Additionally, using a seed-based correlation analysis, we demonstrated a significant inverse relationship between the degree of correlation between the two M1s and GABA concentration (r = −0.60, p=0.047; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a trend towards an inverse relationship between the degree of correlation between left M1 and left PMD and GABA concentration (r = −0.49, p=0.12).
source: There was a trend towards an inverse relationship between the degree of correlation between left M1 and left PMD and GABA concentration (r = −0.49, p=0.12; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, a significant inverse relationship between M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the motor RSN was demonstrated (r = −0.569, p=0.02).
source: (A) A significant inverse relationship between M1-GABA and functional connectivity within the motor RSN was again demonstrated (r = −0.569, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, the relationship between M1-GABA and motor RSN connectivity was anatomically specific (M1-GABA-DMN correlation r = 0.23, p=0.37; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.61; p=0.01).
source: This was both anatomically and neurochemically specific (anatomical specificity: M1-GABA-DMN correlation r = 0.23, p=0.37; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.61; p=0.01; neurochemical specificity: M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation: r = −0.406, p=0.11; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.45; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, the relationship between M1-GABA and motor RSN connectivity was neurochemically specific (M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation: r = −0.406, p=0.11; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.45; p<0.05).
source: This was both anatomically and neurochemically specific (anatomical specificity: M1-GABA-DMN correlation r = 0.23, p=0.37; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.61; p=0.01; neurochemical specificity: M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation: r = −0.406, p=0.11; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.45; p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, a significant inverse relationship between the degree of M1-M1 correlation and M1-GABA was found (r = −0.49, p=0.05).
source: (B) As in experiment 1, a significant inverse relationship between the degree of M1-M1 correlation and M1-GABA was found (r = −0.49, p=0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Experiment 3, the relationship between M1-GABA and the strength of functional connectivity within the motor RSN was maintained in healthy older adults (r = −0.69, p=0.037).
source: (A) Experiment 3 found that the relationship between M1-GABA and the strength of functional connectivity within the motor RSN was maintained in healthy older adults (r = −0.69, p=0.037).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, the relationship between M1-GABA and motor RSN connectivity was anatomically specific (M1-GABA-DMN correlation: r = 0.41, p=0.26; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.22; p=0.03).
source: Similarly to experiments 1 and 2 this relationship was both anatomically and neurochemically specific (anatomical specificity: M1-GABA-DMN correlation: r = 0.41, p=0.26; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.22; p=0.03; neurochemical specificity: M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation r = 0.13, p=0.73; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.79; p=0.04).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, the relationship between M1-GABA and motor RSN connectivity was neurochemically specific (M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation r = 0.13, p=0.73; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.79; p=0.04).
source: Similarly to experiments 1 and 2 this relationship was both anatomically and neurochemically specific (anatomical specificity: M1-GABA-DMN correlation: r = 0.41, p=0.26; M1-GABA-motor vs M1-GABA-DMN: Z = 2.22; p=0.03; neurochemical specificity: M1-Glx-motor RSN correlation r = 0.13, p=0.73; M1-GABA-motor correlation with Glx covaried out: r = −0.79; p=0.04).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, a significant relationship between the degree of M1-M1 correlation and M1-GABA was found (r = −0.62, p=0.035).
source: (B) A significant relationship between the degree of M1-M1 correlation and M1-GABA was again found (r = −0.62, p=0.035).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In Experiment 4, a significant increase in network functional connectivity after tDCS was observed in the motor RSN (pre: 20.7 ± 3.34, post: 26.7 ± 2.97; t(9) = 2.59, p=0.02).
source: A significant increase in network functional connectivity after tDCS was observed in the motor RSN (pre: 20.7 ± 3.34, post: 26.7 ± 2.97; t(9) = 2.59, p=0.02; Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 and shown in Figure 4.

claim: In Experiment 4, there was a significant increase in the degree of M1-M1 correlation after tDCS (t(9) = 1.94, p=0.04).
source: There was also a significant increase in the degree of M1-M1 correlation (t(9) = 1.94, p=0.04; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA is robust, as it is replicated across both ICA and seed-based approaches.
source: We believe that the fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA demonstrated here is robust, as it is replicated across both ICA and seed-based approaches; whether the MRS and fMRI data were collected on the same day or different days; across different scanners; and in young and old healthy cohorts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across multiple experimental conditions and methods.

claim: The fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA is robust whether the MRS and fMRI data were collected on the same day or different days.
source: We believe that the fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA demonstrated here is robust, as it is replicated across both ICA and seed-based approaches; whether the MRS and fMRI data were collected on the same day or different days; across different scanners; and in young and old healthy cohorts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: The fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA is robust across different scanners.
source: We believe that the fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA demonstrated here is robust, as it is replicated across both ICA and seed-based approaches; whether the MRS and fMRI data were collected on the same day or different days; across different scanners; and in young and old healthy cohorts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: The fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA is robust in young and old healthy cohorts.
source: We believe that the fundamental relationship between resting connectivity within the motor network and M1 GABA demonstrated here is robust, as it is replicated across both ICA and seed-based approaches; whether the MRS and fMRI data were collected on the same day or different days; across different scanners; and in young and old healthy cohorts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of results across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: The activity within the motor RSN has been shown to be related to fluctuations in the power of beta oscillations.
source: The activity within the motor RSN has been shown to be related to fluctuations in the power of beta oscillations (Brookes et al., 2011), which have in turn been related to GABA activity (Hall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brookes et al., 2011.

claim: Beta oscillations have been related to GABA activity.
source: The activity within the motor RSN has been shown to be related to fluctuations in the power of beta oscillations (Brookes et al., 2011), which have in turn been related to GABA activity (Hall et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hall et al., 2011.

claim: A simulation-based paper suggested a positive relationship between local oscillatory power in the gamma band and resting state functional connectivity.
source: A recent simulation-based paper suggested a positive relationship between local oscillatory power in the gamma band and resting state functional connectivity (Cabral et al., 2011), something supported in the visual network by a relationship between RSN connectivity and local gamma frequency oscillatory activity (Shmuel and Leopold, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cabral et al., 2011.

claim: In the visual network, there is a relationship between RSN connectivity and local gamma frequency oscillatory activity.
source: A recent simulation-based paper suggested a positive relationship between local oscillatory power in the gamma band and resting state functional connectivity (Cabral et al., 2011), something supported in the visual network by a relationship between RSN connectivity and local gamma frequency oscillatory activity (Shmuel and Leopold, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shmuel and Leopold, 2008.

claim: Evoked gamma power is inversely related to extra-synaptic GABA tone.
source: Evoked gamma power is also known to be inversely related to extra-synaptic GABA tone (Towers et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Towers et al., 2004.

claim: GABA is present in the human brain in three major pools—in pre-synaptic vesicles, as a metabolite in the cytoplasm, and in the extracellular fluid.
source: GABA is present in the human brain in three major pools—in pre-synaptic vesicles, as a metabolite in the cytoplasm, and in the extracellular fluid, where it underlies extra-synaptic GABA tone.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge of GABA distribution in the brain.

claim: Extracellular GABA underlies extra-synaptic GABA tone.
source: GABA is present in the human brain in three major pools—in pre-synaptic vesicles, as a metabolite in the cytoplasm, and in the extracellular fluid, where it underlies extra-synaptic GABA tone.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge of GABA function.

claim: MRS-assessed GABA more closely reflects extra-synaptic rather than synaptic GABA activity.
source: It is likely that MRS-assessed GABA, which is sensitive to the total amount of GABA within the voxel, more closely reflects extra-synaptic rather than synaptic GABA activity (Stagg et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2011b and inference about what MRS measures.

claim: The negative correlation found between motor RSN functional connectivity and MRS-assessed GABA in M1 is consistent with the idea that fluctuations in the power of oscillations underlie long-range resting functional connectivity.
source: While it is not yet clear what the relationship is between local gamma oscillations and beta oscillations, the negative correlation found between motor RSN functional connectivity and MRS-assessed GABA in M1 is consistent with the idea that fluctuations in the power of oscillations underlie long-range resting functional connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and their consistency with theoretical models.

claim: A previous study observed a correlation between GABA in the posteromedial cortex and the strength of the default mode network.
source: One previous study has observed a correlation between GABA in the posteromedial cortex and the strength of the default mode network (Kapogiannis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kapogiannis et al., 2013.

claim: The relationships between GABA and resting state connectivity are not specific to the motor system, but rather a general feature of resting state functional connectivity networks.
source: Taken together with our findings, this suggests that the relationships we report are not specific to the motor system, but rather a general feature of resting state functional connectivity networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous work by Kapogiannis et al., 2013.

claim: Kapogiannis et al. demonstrated a significant positive correlation between glutamate in the posteromedial cortex and the strength of the default mode network.
source: It is interesting to note, however, that in addition to a relationship with GABA, Kapogiannis et al. demonstrate a significant positive correlation between glutamate in the posteromedial cortex and the strength of the default mode network.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from Kapogiannis et al.

claim: A relationship between GABA levels and BOLD signal in response to a task has been demonstrated in anatomically plausible regions for both motor and visual tasks.
source: Other previous studies have explored the relationship between task-evoked BOLD responses and GABA: a relationship between GABA levels and BOLD signal in response to a task has been demonstrated in anatomically plausible regions for both motor and visual tasks (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009; Stagg et al., 2011a), such that higher local GABA concentrations are associated with smaller task-related BOLD signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009 and Stagg et al., 2011a.

claim: Higher local GABA concentrations are associated with smaller task-related BOLD signals.
source: Other previous studies have explored the relationship between task-evoked BOLD responses and GABA: a relationship between GABA levels and BOLD signal in response to a task has been demonstrated in anatomically plausible regions for both motor and visual tasks (Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009; Stagg et al., 2011a), such that higher local GABA concentrations are associated with smaller task-related BOLD signals.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muthukumaraswamy et al., 2009 and Stagg et al., 2011a.

claim: Motor-task related BOLD signals correlate with the strength of the motor RSN across individuals.
source: Motor-task related BOLD signals have also been shown to correlate with the strength of the motor RSN across individuals (Kannurpatti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kannurpatti et al., 2012.

claim: Motor learning decreases GABA.
source: The relationships demonstrated here, build on this prior work and provide a mechanistic explanation for the previous finding that motor learning, which decreases GABA (Floyer-Lea et al., 2006), increases RSN functional connectivity (Albert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Floyer-Lea et al., 2006.

claim: Motor learning increases RSN functional connectivity.
source: The relationships demonstrated here, build on this prior work and provide a mechanistic explanation for the previous finding that motor learning, which decreases GABA (Floyer-Lea et al., 2006), increases RSN functional connectivity (Albert et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Albert et al., 2009.

claim: The findings relate RSN functional connectivity to local inhibitory tone within the motor cortex.
source: Taken together, these findings relate RSN functional connectivity to local inhibitory tone within the motor cortex, and thereby may reveal an important neural mechanistic explanation for the RSN changes observed in a wide range of states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: All neurochemicals of interest were expressed as a ratio to N-acetyl aspartate (NAA).
source: MR Spectroscopy data were acquired from the hand region of left primary motor cortex (M1) and all neurochemicals of interest were expressed as a ratio to N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) (Stagg et al., 2009; see Figure 1 for representative spectra).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used, supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2009.

claim: Experiment 1 included 12 volunteers (6 male; mean age 23 years [range 21–31 years]).
source: 12 volunteers (6 male; mean age 23 years [range 21–31 years]) participated.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: In Experiment 1, MRS data was acquired using a 1 channel transmit/receive head-coil from a 2 × 2 × 2 cm voxel centred on the hand-knob area within the motor cortex in the left hemisphere.
source: MRS data was acquired using a 1 channel transmit/receive head-coil from a 2 × 2 × 2 cm voxel centred on the hand-knob area within the motor cortex in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Experiment 2 included 16 volunteers (2 male, mean age 24 years, [range 20–39 years]).
source: MRS and fMRI data were acquired from 16 volunteers (2 male, mean age 24 years, [range 20–39 years]) on a 3T Siemens Verio in the same session using a 32 channel receive coil.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Experiment 3 included 12 volunteers (6 male, mean age 61 years [range 45–72 years]).
source: 12 volunteers (6 male, mean age 61 years [range 45–72 years]) participated.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Experiment 4 included 10 volunteers (3 male, mean age 22.7 years [range 21–24 years]).
source: 10 volunteers (3 male, mean age 22.7 years [range 21–24 years]) participated.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: In Experiment 4, anodal tDCS was delivered at 1 mA for 10 min.
source: Anodal, facilitatory, tDCS was delivered via a DC stimulator (Eldith GmbH; Germany), the current had a ramp-up time of 10 s, was held at 1 mA for 10 min and then ramped down over 10s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Any spectra with a NAA linewidth of >10Hz were rejected as being of insufficient quality.
source: Any spectra with a NAA linewidth of >10Hz were rejected as being of insufficient quality (Stagg et al., 2009) (one subject from experiment 1 and three from experiment 3).
evidence: This is a description of the data quality control method, supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2009.

claim: One subject from experiment 1 was rejected due to poor spectral quality.
source: Any spectra with a NAA linewidth of >10Hz were rejected as being of insufficient quality (Stagg et al., 2009) (one subject from experiment 1 and three from experiment 3).
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion.

claim: Three subjects from experiment 3 were rejected due to poor spectral quality.
source: Any spectra with a NAA linewidth of >10Hz were rejected as being of insufficient quality (Stagg et al., 2009) (one subject from experiment 1 and three from experiment 3).
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion.

claim: All neurotransmitter concentrations are corrected for grey matter and white matter concentration.
source: All neurotransmitter concentrations are given as a ratio to NAA and corrected for grey matter and white matter concentration as described previously using a T1-weighted high-resolution structural scan acquired immediately prior to the MRS acquisition (Stagg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method, supported by citation to Stagg et al., 2009.

claim: Effects of head motion on resting state connectivity are greatly ameliorated by the dual regression approach compared against simpler single-regression-based analyses.
source: Motion is known to have complex effects on resting state connectivity on a subject-by-subject basis (Power et al., 2012), but effects of head motion are greatly ameliorated by the dual regression approach used here, compared against simpler single-regression-based analyses (Zuo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Power et al., 2012 and Zuo et al., 2010.

claim: Motion has complex effects on resting state connectivity on a subject-by-subject basis.
source: Motion is known to have complex effects on resting state connectivity on a subject-by-subject basis (Power et al., 2012), but effects of head motion are greatly ameliorated by the dual regression approach used here, compared against simpler single-regression-based analyses (Zuo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Power et al., 2012.
